profile.summary: Judges record the history of the community of Israel in the period of the judges, from Otniel to Eli, covering about 299 years, according to the count mentioned in the introduction. The book brings together, first, the sequence of the main leaders raised by God to liberate the people and face their corruption, and then, in the final chapters, some striking episodes that took place in those days, without knowing how much judge happened. The work presents a privileged people by the covenant, but repeatedly unfaithful, which results in external oppression, internal disorder and strong contrast between the call of God and the moral reality of the nation. The authorship is traditionally associated with the prophet Samuel by some ancient interpreters, but the introduction treats this as a probable opinion, not certainty.
profile.setting: Israel, in the period between the conquest of Canaan and the establishment of the monarchy, when there was no king in Israel and the government was occasionally exercised by judges raised by God. The scenario is tribal, decentralized and often marked by conflicts with neighboring peoples, as well as internal tensions and religious corruption. Although there is political and moral disorder, the introduction presupposes the continuity of the service of the tabernacle according to the law of Moses and the presence of many who still attended him.

structure.label: History of the judges of Israel
structure.description: An orderly report of the main leaders and deliveries, from Otniel to Samson, showing the occasional performance of the judges and the alternation between oppression, liberation and rest periods.

structure.label: Final episodes of the time of the judges
structure.description: Set of particular and memorable events, gathered at the end not to interrupt the thread of the main narrative, without the introduction determining with certainty in which days of which judge occurred.

themes: Israel's infidelity despite the privileges of the covenant
God's sovereignty by raising judges for deliverance and correction
The disorder produced when there is no stable government and each one does what seems right to him
The permanence of true worship in the midst of national corruption
The limitation of every earthly order and the need to wait for the fullness of righteousness in God
readingKeys: Notice the recurring pattern of sin, oppression, clamor and liberation, which structures the narrative.
Note that the judges do not act as permanent government, but as instruments raised on specific occasions by God.
Read the final chapters as episodes attached to the large historical frame, gathered to preserve the general sequence of the book.
profile.cautions: The introduction presents the book as a selective history of the judges' period and not as a complete record of all that took place in Israel. The authorship is attributed by an ancient interpreter to the prophet Samuel, but this is not affirmed as certainty. Nor should it be assumed that the years mentioned for the judges are all strictly consecutive, as some periods of servitude may coincide with the years of the judges themselves.

dossier.narratedEra: Period of judges in Israel, from Otniel to Eli, as summarized in the introduction. The source reads this was like the time when, especially God, was the king of Israel, while the judges appeared occasionally to rid the people and purify them from idolatry. The last five chapters are presented as private episodes that occurred on the days in which the judges judged, without safe identification of the judge in whose time they happened.
dossier.compositionEra: The source does not inform date of composition. She only records Bishop Patrick's opinion that the prophet Samuel would have been the author of the book. Therefore, the date of writing remains unspecified in this source, and traditional authorship appears only as a proposal mentioned, not as demonstrated conclusion.

politics.title: Occasional, non-continuous government
politics.detail: The introduction states that the "governance of the judges" was not constant, but occasional: they were raised up by the Spirit of God for a public mission when needed. His role included avenging Israel from enemies and purifying him from idolatries.
politics.readingImpact: This makes the book read as a succession of divine crises and interventions, not as a stable history of administration.

politics.title: Absence of central monarchy
politics.detail: Henry emphasizes that in this period there was no permanent human king; God was in a special way the king of Israel. The reading of the time ends with the maxim that, without king in Israel, each one did what seemed right in his own eyes.
politics.readingImpact: The political context explains the tone of the book's disorder and helps to understand why the introduction contrasts judges and royalty.

politics.title: Tribal fragmentation
politics.detail: The source says that each tribe seems to have ruled much in their own way, acting separately, without a common head or unified council. This would have produced many internal differences and prevented more expressive actions.
politics.readingImpact: History is now read as marked by political dispersion, which helps to explain the difficulty of national unity in the period.

politics.title: Explicit foreign depressions
politics.detail: The introduction cites, as examples, the oppression of Eglom for eighteen years and Jabin for twenty years, inserted in the context of the servids that overlap the times of the judges.
politics.readingImpact: The book is not only about internal leadership, but also of recurring external military pressure, which shapes the need for the liberators.

politics.title: Tribal distribution of judges
politics.detail: Henry notes that the judges came from eight different tribes, and that the honor ended up focusing on Judah. He also mentions that Eli and Samuel, outside the main clipping of the book, were from Levi.
politics.readingImpact: This highlights the tribal diversity of leadership and prevents reading the book as if there was a fixed ruling elite from the beginning.

customs.title: Service of the tabernacle maintained
customs.detail: Despite the corruption described, the introduction holds that there was a face of religion on the earth and that the service of the tabernacle, according to the law of Moses, continued in force; many attended it.
customs.readingImpact: The reader is led to see that the scenario was not of total abandonment of the faith, but of coexistence between legitimate cult and idolatry.
customs.reference: Exodus -Numbers; no specific biblical reference cited in the introduction

customs.title: Unregistered everyday life
customs.detail: Henry notes that historians usually do not record the common course of a nation's justice and trade, taking it as a presupposition; they highlight wars and disturbances. Observation is used to remember that there was ordinary life beyond the narrated conflicts.
customs.readingImpact: This prevents the book from being read as a total portrait of society; much of its civil routine remains silent in the narrative.
customs.reference: without specific biblical reference cited in the introduction

customs.title: Local justice and performance of Deborah
customs.detail: The introduction mentions that Deborah, as a prophetess, was sought throughout Israel for trial even before his military performance, which suggests a recognized civil-religious role.
customs.readingImpact: The context shows that the function of "judge" could include mediation and advice before involving war, extending the reading of Judges 4:4.

customs.title: Autonomous tribal organization
customs.detail: Each tribe seems to have acted within its own sphere, without a common center of government. This tribal autonomy is presented as a daily trait of political and social life.
customs.readingImpact: It helps to understand why the book shows difficult cooperation and local responses, rather than continuous national coordination.

language.title: Names of the book in different traditions
language.detail: The introduction calls the book Shepher Shophtim in Hebrew, records the Syriac and Arabic enlargement (Book of the Judges of the Sons of Israel) and notes that the Septuagint simply calls it Kritai, "Judges."
language.readingImpact: These designations guide the reading to the institutional character of the book and show how the tradition of translation already interpreted its content.
language.reference: without specific biblical reference cited in the introduction

language.title: Functional meaning of "julgar"
language.detail: Henry defines the judges in this book not as magistrates in the modern sense, but as leaders aroused for two main tasks: to rid Israel of enemies and correct their idolatries.
language.readingImpact: This avoids legal anachronism and makes the reader see the role of judges as a liberator, disciplinary and spiritual.

language.title: Literary structure with final appendix
language.detail: The introduction states that the last five chapters were put at the end so that the thread of general history would not be interrupted. She also places episodes similar to those of Ruth within the same period, though without defining the exact judge.
language.readingImpact: The reader should read Jz 17'21 as material intentionally grouped at the end, not as a continuous chronological sequence of the main narrative.

language.title: Contrast rhetorical between corruption and order
language.detail: Henry describes the people as "miserably corrupted" and "miserably oppressed," and resumes the formula that each one did what seemed right in his own eyes.
language.readingImpact: Language accentuates the moral diagnosis of the period and prepares the theological reading of Judges as a time of disorder and necessity of divine intervention.

timeline.title: Estimated total period of 299 years
timeline.detail: According to the computation of Dr. Lightfoot quoted by Henry, the story of Judges covers 299 years, from Otniel to Samson, with the mention of Eli and Samuel outside the main book.
timeline.readingImpact: The period ceases to be only a wide era and is presented as a relatively defined chronological sequence, although dependent on this specific account.

timeline.title: Individual durations of judges
timeline.detail: The introduction lists the periods attributed to several judges: Otniel 40 years, Ehud 80, Barak 40, Gideon 40, Abimelech 3, Tola 23, Jair 22, Jefté 6, Ibsã 7, Elom 10, Abdom 8 and Samson 20.
timeline.readingImpact: The internal chronology of the book is read as a succession of administrations and deliveries, although the sum depends on the organization proposed by the source.

timeline.title: Serdões overlap with judges
timeline.detail: Henry claims that the years of oppression - such as those of Eglon and Jabin - must be counted so as to fit into some of the years of the judges, and not necessarily in a separate sequence.
timeline.readingImpact: This alerts the reader not to assemble a simplistic chronology; the text admits overlap between oppression and leadership.

timeline.title: Final chapters and the time of judges
timeline.detail: The last five chapters are situated in the general period "in which the judges ruled," but the introduction says that it is not certain in which specific judge this occurred. She further mentions that Ruth 1:1 belongs at the same time wide.
timeline.readingImpact: He avoids dating Jz 17'21 with excessive precision and keeps these accounts within the general picture of the judges' period.

investigation: To compare the traditional authorship attributed to Samuel with the observation that the source only records this opinion, without dating the composition.
Read Jz 17-21 as the final narrative appendix, observing how the introduction justifies this literary placement.
Mapping as the tribal distribution of judges, according to Henry, reinforces Israel's political fragmentation in the period.
Evaluating the formula "each one did what seemed right in his own eyes" as theological synthesis of the book, not as a total description of society.
dossier.limits: This dossier depends solely on the introduction of Matthew Henry provided here. Therefore, there is no external historiographical independence or other proposals of authorship, dating or chronology other than those mentioned in the source. The 299-year count is presented as Dr. Lightfoot, and Samuel's author appears only as the opinion of Bishop Patrick. Many observations on justice, commerce, everyday life and tribal organization are inferences of the introduction, not detailed descriptions of the biblical text or autonomous historical proofs. There is also no direct discussion of larger empires, absolute dates or all cultural practices of the period.
